course: Daily Milk Sales: Dairy Herd System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: The lactation curve is the pattern of milk production from a cow from the day she calves until she dries off. For a dairy herd system selling milk daily, understanding this curve is the difference between profit and loss. A healthy cow typically peaks in milk yield about 6 to 8 weeks after calving, producing up to 20-30 litres per day for a crossbreed like Friesian x Zebu. After that peak, production slowly declines by about 5-10% each month. If you know the curve, you can plan feed, labour, and sales. For example, a cow giving 20 litres at peak will give about 15 litres at month 4 and 10 litres at month 8. Without this knowledge, you might overfeed or underfeed, leading to thin cows and low milk. In Africa, where many farmers rely on daily milk sales for cash flow, missing the peak means missing the highest income period. Also, the curve helps you decide when to rebreed. A cow should be bred again 60-90 days after calving to maintain a 12-13 month calving interval. If she is not bred, her lactation extends but total daily milk drops, and you lose money. The curve also signals health problems: a sudden drop can mean mastitis, foot rot, or poor feed. By recording daily milk with a simple notebook or a phone app, you learn your herd's normal curve. Then you can act fast. In this module, you will learn the tools, steps, mistakes, safety, and practice to master the lactation curve for your daily milk sales.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To track and manage the lactation curve, you need simple, affordable tools. First, a milk record book or a notebook with columns for date, cow ID, morning milk (litres), evening milk (litres), and total. A hardcover notebook costs less than 5,000 shillings and lasts a year. Second, a measuring jug or graduated bucket, preferably plastic with clear markings up to 30 litres. Metal buckets can dent and hide markings. Third, a permanent marker to label the bucket with cow ID if you have multiple cows. Fourth, a calendar or wall chart to mark calving dates and breeding dates. You can use a simple wall calendar and a red pen. Fifth, a weighing scale for feed, because feed affects the curve. A hanging scale up to 50 kg is useful. Sixth, a thermometer to check for fever if milk drops suddenly. Seventh, a phone with a calculator and a simple app like 'Dairy Record' or even a spreadsheet. If you have no smartphone, a notebook is enough. Eighth, a feed chart showing how much concentrate and forage each cow needs at different lactation stages. For example, a cow giving 20 litres needs about 1 kg of dairy meal per 2.5 litres of milk plus 2 kg for maintenance. Ninth, a body condition score (BCS) chart: you can print one from the internet or draw simple silhouettes. Tenth, a first-aid kit for udder injuries: antiseptic, cotton wool, and gloves. Finally, a whiteboard or chalkboard in the milking shed to write today's totals and compare to yesterday. All these tools cost less than 20,000 shillings total and are available in local agro-vet shops or markets. With them, you can plot your cow's lactation curve on graph paper or just list weekly averages.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to track and use the lactation curve. Step 1: Record calving date. Write it on the calendar and in your notebook. This is day 0. Step 2: Measure milk every milking. Use your graduated bucket. Record morning and evening yields separately. Do this for at least the first 10 days, then weekly if labour is tight. Step 3: Calculate daily total and weekly average. Add morning and evening. For a week, sum all daily totals and divide by 7. Step 4: Plot the curve. On graph paper, put weeks on the x-axis and litres on the y-axis. Mark each weekly average. You will see a rise to peak around week 6-8, then a gradual decline. Step 5: Compare to expected. For a crossbreed, peak should be 15-25 litres. If peak is below 10 litres, check feed, water, and health. Step 6: Adjust feed. As milk rises, increase concentrate by 0.5 kg for every extra litre above 10 litres. For example, if she gives 20 litres, feed 4 kg dairy meal plus 2 kg for maintenance = 6 kg per day, split into two feeds. Step 7: Monitor decline. After peak, milk drops about 5% per month. If it drops more than 10% in a month, investigate: mastitis, worms, or heat stress. Step 8: Decide breeding date. At 60-90 days after calving, if the cow is healthy and giving above 10 litres, breed her. Step 9: Dry off at 7 months pregnant or when milk falls below 5 litres per day. Step 10: Review records. At drying off, calculate total milk for the lactation. Compare to previous lactations. Use this to cull poor producers and keep good ones. Repeat for each cow. This method works for one cow or fifty. The key is consistency: record every day, even if you only note totals.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: Not recording milk daily. Many farmers guess. Fix: Keep a notebook in the milking shed. Write with a pencil if ink runs. Mistake 2: Feeding the same amount all year. A cow at peak needs more feed than a dry cow. Fix: Use the 1 kg dairy meal per 2.5 litres rule. Adjust weekly. Mistake 3: Ignoring sudden drops. A drop of 3 litres in one day can mean mastitis. Fix: Check udder for heat, swelling, or clots. Strip milk onto a dark cloth to see clots. Call a vet if fever. Mistake 4: Breeding too late. Waiting beyond 90 days reduces lifetime milk. Fix: Mark calendar 60 days after calving. If cow is healthy, breed at observed heat. Mistake 5: Overmilking or incomplete milking. This reduces yield and causes mastitis. Fix: Milk until udder is soft, but no longer than 8 minutes per cow. Use clean hands and a clean bucket. Mistake 6: Poor water access. A cow giving 20 litres needs 80-100 litres of water daily. Fix: Provide clean water at all times. A trough with a float valve is best. Mistake 7: Heat stress. In hot African afternoons, milk drops. Fix: Provide shade, fans, or sprinklers. Mistake 8: Not drying off properly. Cows that are milked until calving have weak calves and low next lactation. Fix: Dry off 60 days before expected calving. Reduce milking frequency over one week. Mistake 9: Using wrong BCS. Thin cows (BCS below 2.5) give less milk. Fix: Score monthly. Feed extra to thin cows. Mistake 10: No records for individual cows. You cannot cull poor performers. Fix: Use ear tags or names. Record per cow. Each mistake has a simple fix. Start with daily recording and correct feeding.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety first: When handling cows for milking or checking the lactation curve, wear clean overalls and boots. Wash hands with soap before milking. Use a clean bucket and a strip cup to check for mastitis. Never milk a cow with a fever or obvious udder infection without gloves. If you suspect mastitis, isolate the cow and milk her last. Dispose of infected milk properly; do not sell it. Best practice for record keeping: Use a pencil and a notebook that stays in the milking shed. At the end of each week, transfer totals to a master sheet. Keep records for at least three lactations. This helps you see patterns. Best practice for feeding: Weigh feed, don't guess. Use a hanging scale. Store feed in dry, raised place to avoid mould. Mouldy feed can cause abortion and milk drop. Best practice for water: Clean troughs daily. A cow drinks 3-5 litres per litre of milk. So a 20-litre cow needs 60-100 litres. Best practice for milking hygiene: Use a single-use paper towel or clean cloth to dry udder. Use teat dip after milking. This prevents mastitis. Best practice for breeding: Keep a breeding calendar. Observe heat twice daily for 30 minutes. Record all heats. If a cow is not bred by 90 days, consult an AI technician. Best practice for drying off: Reduce milking gradually over 7 days. Give dry cow therapy if available. Best practice for heat stress: Provide shade trees or a simple roof. Sprinklers in the afternoon can increase milk by 10-15%. Best practice for safety of people: Never stand directly behind a cow. Use a crush or head gate for examinations. Keep children away from bulls. Finally, keep a first-aid kit with antiseptic, bandages, and gloves. If you get kicked or injured, clean the wound and seek medical help. Following these practices keeps you, your cows, and your milk safe.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: For this exercise, you will track one cow's lactation curve for 4 weeks. If you have no cow, borrow records from a neighbour or use the example below. Step 1: Choose a cow that calved 1-2 weeks ago. Write her ID and calving date. Step 2: Every milking (morning and evening), measure milk with your graduated bucket. Record in a notebook. Step 3: At the end of each day, add morning and evening. Write the total. Step 4: At the end of each week, calculate the average daily milk for that week. Example: Week 1: 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16 litres = total 99 litres / 7 = 14.1 litres average. Week 2: 16, 17, 18, 18, 19, 19, 20 = 127 / 7 = 18.1 litres. Week 3: 20, 20, 21, 21, 20, 20, 19 = 141 / 7 = 20.1 litres. Week 4: 19, 19, 18, 18, 17, 17, 16 = 124 / 7 = 17.7 litres. Step 5: Plot these averages on graph paper. You will see a peak at week 3 (20.1 litres) then a decline. Step 6: Compare to expected peak of 6-8 weeks. If your cow peaks earlier or lower, note possible reasons: feed, water, health. Step 7: Calculate feed needed. At peak of 20 litres, feed 20/2.5 = 8 kg dairy meal? No, rule is 1 kg per 2.5 litres above maintenance. Maintenance is 2 kg. So total = 2 + (20/2.5) = 2 + 8 = 10 kg? That is too high. Correct rule: 1 kg dairy meal per 2.5 litres of milk total, but not less than 2 kg. For 20 litres, 20/2.5 = 8 kg. That is correct for high producers. If that is too expensive, feed 1 kg per 3 litres. Step 8: Write a short report: cow ID, peak week, peak litres, average for 4 weeks, and any health issues. Step 9: Discuss with a fellow farmer or extension officer. Step 10: Repeat for another cow. This exercise teaches you to see the curve and make decisions. Do it for at least one full lactation to master it.

quiz.q: What is the lactation curve?
options: A) The shape of a cow's udder
B) The pattern of milk production from calving to drying off
C) The amount of feed a cow eats per day
quiz.explanation: The lactation curve describes how milk yield rises to a peak and then gradually declines over the lactation period.

quiz.q: When does a healthy cow typically peak in milk production?
quiz.explanation: Most cows reach peak milk yield about 6 to 8 weeks after calving.

quiz.q: Why is understanding the lactation curve important for daily milk sales?
options: A) It helps you plan feed, labour, and sales
B) It tells you when to sell the cow
D) It determines the colour of milk
quiz.explanation: Knowing the curve allows you to match resources and income to the cow's production cycle.

quiz.q: What is a typical peak milk yield for a Friesian x Zebu crossbreed?
quiz.explanation: Crossbreeds like Friesian x Zebu often peak at 15-25 litres per day under good management.

quiz.q: After peak, milk production typically declines by what percentage each month?
quiz.explanation: A gradual decline of about 5-10% per month is normal after peak.

quiz.q: What is the recommended breeding interval for a dairy cow?
quiz.explanation: A 12-13 month calving interval is ideal, meaning rebreeding 60-90 days after calving.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for measuring milk yield?
options: B) A graduated bucket or measuring jug
C) A weighing scale for feed
quiz.explanation: A graduated bucket allows accurate measurement of milk volume.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of dairy meal per 2.5 litres of milk?
quiz.explanation: The common rule is 1 kg of dairy meal for every 2.5 litres of milk produced.

quiz.q: How much water does a cow giving 20 litres of milk need daily?
quiz.explanation: A cow needs about 3-5 litres of water per litre of milk, so 20 litres milk requires 60-100 litres water.

quiz.q: What should you do if a cow's milk drops suddenly by 3 litres in one day?
options: B) Check for mastitis and other health issues
quiz.explanation: A sudden drop often indicates mastitis, foot rot, or other health problems requiring immediate attention.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in managing the lactation curve?
options: B) Feeding the same amount all year
quiz.explanation: Feeding a constant amount ignores the cow's changing needs during lactation.

quiz.q: How can you prevent heat stress in dairy cows?
options: D) Keep cows in dark shed
quiz.explanation: Shade and cooling methods like sprinklers help maintain milk yield in hot weather.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to dry off a cow?
options: B) Reduce milking gradually over 7 days
quiz.explanation: Gradual reduction over a week helps prevent mastitis and allows the udder to involute.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record milk per individual cow?
options: A) To know which cows to cull
quiz.explanation: Individual records help identify poor producers for culling and good ones for retention.

quiz.q: What safety practice should you follow when milking?
options: A) Wear clean overalls and wash hands
B) Milk cows with mastitis first
D) Stand directly behind the cow
quiz.explanation: Clean hands and clothing reduce the risk of mastitis and milk contamination.

quiz.q: What is a body condition score (BCS) used for?
options: B) To assess cow's fat reserves
quiz.explanation: BCS estimates body fat, which affects milk production and health.

quiz.q: What should you do with milk from a cow with mastitis?
quiz.explanation: Milk from mastitic cows contains bacteria and antibiotics and should not be sold or fed.

quiz.q: How often should you observe cows for heat?
quiz.explanation: Observing heat twice daily for 30 minutes helps detect standing heat for timely breeding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended drying off period before calving?
quiz.explanation: A 60-day dry period allows udder tissue to regenerate for the next lactation.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, what should you plot on the graph?
quiz.explanation: Plotting weekly average milk yield shows the shape of the lactation curve.

quiz.q: What is the maintenance feed requirement for a dairy cow?
quiz.explanation: About 2 kg of dairy meal is needed for maintenance before production.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of good milking hygiene?
options: A) Using teat dip after milking
quiz.explanation: Teat dipping after milking helps prevent mastitis.

quiz.q: What can cause a sudden drop in milk yield?
quiz.explanation: Mastitis, foot rot, and poor feed are all common causes of sudden milk drop.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records for at least three lactations?
options: A) To see patterns and make culling decisions
quiz.explanation: Long-term records reveal each cow's production potential and health trends.

quiz.q: What is the correct action if a cow is not bred by 90 days after calving?
quiz.explanation: Consulting a technician helps identify and solve fertility problems.

quiz.q: How can you reduce the risk of mouldy feed?
options: A) Store feed in a dry, raised place
B) Keep feed on the floor
quiz.explanation: Dry, raised storage prevents moisture and mould growth.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of providing shade in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: Shade reduces heat stress, which can improve milk yield by 10-15%.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, what is the peak week in the example?
quiz.explanation: The example shows peak average of 20.1 litres in week 3.

quiz.q: What should you do before milking a cow with suspected mastitis?
options: B) Milk her last and wear gloves
D) Use same cloth as others
quiz.explanation: Milking infected cows last and using gloves prevents spread of infection.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a strip cup?
options: B) To check for clots indicating mastitis
quiz.explanation: A strip cup is used to examine foremilk for clots or flakes, signs of mastitis.
